title: Online Poker Tells in Canada: Timing and Bet Sizing
excerpt: You cannot see faces online, but the information is still there. A guide to timing tells, bet sizing patterns and table habits for Canadian poker players.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
The standard line is that online poker tells do not exist — no faces, no shaking hands, no chip fumbling, so nothing to read. It is a comfortable belief and it is wrong. Online play strips away the physical layer and replaces it with something arguably more reliable: a precise, timestamped record of every decision your opponent has made, how long it took them, and exactly how much they chose to bet.

Physical tells are noisy and frequently misread. Timing and sizing patterns are quantitative, repeatable, and much harder for an opponent to disguise. For Canadian players grinding cash games or tournaments, learning to read them is one of the cheapest edges available — it costs nothing but attention.

Timing tells: what the clock says

Every action carries a duration, and duration correlates with the decision behind it. The correlations are not universal, but they hold often enough at low and mid stakes to be worth acting on.

The instant call. A call that lands in under a second usually means a hand that is neither strong enough to raise nor weak enough to fold. Draws, weak pairs, and marginal made hands live here. The speed itself is the giveaway: the player had already decided before the action reached them, which means their hand had no difficult decision in it. Instant calls are an invitation to keep betting on later streets.

The instant bet or raise. Often polarised in the opposite direction. Snap-raises frequently indicate a pre-planned action — either a very strong hand the player intended to raise with regardless, or a bluff that was decided upon before the card fell. Context separates them: a snap-raise on a scary board after a passive line is far more often a made hand than a bluff.

The long tank followed by a bet. Genuine strength is rarer here than people assume. Value hands usually know they are betting; the deliberation is more often a player calculating whether a bluff is worth attempting, or sizing an unfamiliar spot. Treat a long delay before a large bet with more suspicion than a quick one.

The long tank followed by a check or a call. This usually is what it looks like — a genuinely close decision with a marginal holding. It is one of the more honest signals at the table.

The caveats that keep you honest

Multi-tabling ruins timing reads. A player running twelve tables acts on a rhythm dictated by their queue, not by hand strength, and their tank may simply be another table's decision. If you suspect an opponent is playing many tables — steady action speeds regardless of situation, no chat, standard sizings — discount timing information heavily. Our guide to online poker strategy covers how multi-table play changes decision patterns on both sides of the equation.

Connection quality is a second confounder, and deliberate deception is a third. Strong regulars randomise their timing precisely because they know it leaks. Timing tells are most valuable against recreational opponents and least valuable against the people you most want an edge on.

Bet sizing: the loudest signal at the table

Sizing tells are more durable than timing tells because they are harder to randomise without cost. A player who wants to disguise sizing must sometimes bet the wrong amount for their hand, which costs real money. Most recreational players never make that trade.

The patterns to watch for:

  • The oversized river bet. Against unbalanced opponents, an unusually large river bet is more often a genuinely strong hand than a bluff. Recreational players size up when they want a call and down when they are afraid.
  • The tiny stab. A quarter-pot bet on a dry flop, particularly from a player who has shown no aggression, is usually a probe rather than value — asking a question cheaply.
  • Sizing that changes with hand strength. The most common leak in low-stakes poker. Track a player across a session: if their pot-sized bets show down monsters and their half-pot bets show down middling hands, you have a full read on their range with no further work required.
  • The min-raise. At micro and low stakes, this frequently signals a premium hand from an inexperienced player trying to build a pot without scaring anyone off.
  • The overbet shove on a completed draw. Almost always exactly what it appears to be from a non-regular.

Build sizing reads deliberately. When a hand goes to showdown, note what the bet sizes were and what the holding turned out to be. Three or four of those observations per opponent is enough to start exploiting a pattern.

Table-behaviour tells beyond the cards

A handful of non-betting signals carry information too:

  • Auto-action checkboxes. When a player uses "check/fold" or "call any" pre-selections, their action lands the instant the previous one completes — noticeably faster than a manual click. That timing signature tells you they had committed before seeing the full picture.
  • Buy-in and rebuy behaviour. A player who reloads to a non-standard amount, or who plays short-stacked, is often signalling either a specific strategy or a bankroll under pressure. Both are exploitable, though differently.
  • Chat. Frustrated commentary after a lost pot is the closest online equivalent to visible tilt, and tilt is more profitable to identify than any individual hand read.
  • Session length and time of day. Late-session players make more errors. Late-night tables in any Canadian time zone run softer than weekday afternoon games.

Protecting your own information

Everything above works against you as well. The basic defences are cheap: use a consistent action delay rather than snapping every decision, avoid pre-selected action boxes in meaningful pots, and standardise your bet sizings so that the same fraction of pot represents both your value hands and your bluffs. Silence in chat costs nothing and gives away nothing.

Note that software-based assistance is a separate question with its own rules. Poker sites in regulated Canadian markets place clear restrictions on what tracking and assistance tools are permitted at the tables, and those rules differ between operators and between provinces. Reading opponents in real time is entirely within the rules; automating that reading may not be.

Putting it to work

Do not try to track everything at once. Pick one opponent per session — ideally the player to your left, whose decisions affect you most — and watch only their bet sizing for an hour. Note the sizes and the showdowns. You will usually find a pattern within a couple of dozen hands, and once found, it does not go away.

Timing and sizing reads are supplements to solid fundamentals, not substitutes for them.
